outline.chapter_title: Mathematical Reasoning and the DeepSeekMath Agenda
outline.description: This chapter introduces mathematical reasoning as a core challenge for language models, explains why open models have lagged behind proprietary systems, and presents DeepSeekMath as a case study in closing that gap through better data and reinforcement learning.
subtopics: Why mathematical reasoning is difficult for language models
The gap between open-source and closed-source math-capable models
What DeepSeekMath aims to achieve
The three-stage system: DeepSeekMath-Base, DeepSeekMath-Instruct, and DeepSeekMath-RL
Headline results, including 51.7% on MATH and 60.9% with self-consistency over 64 samples
The paper's two central ideas: large-scale math pre-training and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)
How this work fits into broader research on reasoning, code, and alignment

outline.description: Before studying the model itself, this chapter builds the conceptual toolkit needed to understand the paper, including pre-training, chain-of-thought prompting, tool use, reinforcement learning, and the benchmarks used throughout the study.
subtopics: Continual pre-training versus supervised fine-tuning versus reinforcement learning
Why code-trained models may be strong starting points for reasoning
Chain-of-thought prompting for step-by-step solutions
Program-of-thought prompting and Python-based problem solving
Tool-integrated reasoning and the role of external computation
Core reinforcement learning ideas: policy, reward, advantage, and KL regularization
Few-shot, zero-shot, Pass@K, Maj@K, and self-consistency
English mathematical benchmarks: GSM8K, MATH, SAT, OCW Courses, and MMLU-STEM
Chinese mathematical benchmarks: MGSM-zh, CMATH, Gaokao-MathCloze, and Gaokao-MathQA
Formal mathematics benchmarks such as miniF2F with Isabelle
General capability benchmarks: MMLU, BBH, HumanEval, and MBPP

outline.chapter_title: Mining Mathematical Data from Common Crawl
outline.description: This chapter explains how the DeepSeekMath Corpus is built from noisy web data using an iterative retrieval and filtering pipeline, showing how a small seed set can be expanded into a large high-quality domain corpus.
subtopics: Why Common Crawl is an attractive source for large-scale domain data
Using OpenWebMath as the initial seed corpus
Training a fastText classifier with positive and negative examples
Deduplication and near-deduplication of raw web pages
Ranking candidate pages by classifier score and selecting top-scoring content
Choosing data volume through pre-training experiments on 40B, 80B, 120B, and 160B tokens
Domain-level analysis to discover new math-rich websites
Human annotation of math-related URL patterns within selected domains
Iterative classifier improvement across four collection rounds
The final corpus: 35.5M pages and 120B math-related tokens
Why the same pipeline could generalize to other domains such as code

outline.description: A good corpus is not only large but also clean, diverse, and benchmark-safe. This chapter studies how DeepSeekMath validates its data and why corpus quality matters as much as model size.
subtopics: Benchmark contamination and why it threatens fair evaluation
N-gram-based decontamination for English and Chinese benchmarks
Comparison corpora: MathPile, OpenWebMath, and Proof-Pile-2
Controlled corpus-quality experiments using DeepSeek-LLM 1.3B
Training settings for fair corpus comparison
Evidence that DeepSeekMath Corpus has higher average quality than competing corpora
Multilingual coverage and why it helps Chinese mathematical reasoning
Scale effects and learning curves for large versus small math corpora
Why repeated training on small corpora quickly plateaus
What the validation experiments imply about data-centric model improvement

outline.description: This chapter details how the base model is constructed, why the authors initialize from a code model, and how a carefully balanced training mixture produces a strong reasoning-oriented foundation model.
subtopics: Why initialize from DeepSeek-Coder-Base-v1.5 7B instead of a general model
The intuition behind code-first then math-focused training
The 500B-token continual pre-training run
Training mixture composition: math corpus, AlgebraicStack, arXiv, GitHub code, and natural language data
Optimizer, learning-rate schedule, context length, and batch size
Balancing specialization in mathematics with retention of coding ability
How continual pre-training differs from task-specific fine-tuning
Expected benefits of multilingual and mixed-modality training data

outline.chapter_title: Evaluating the Base Model Across Mathematics, Proof, and General Reasoning
outline.description: This chapter examines what DeepSeekMath-Base can do before alignment, showing how math pre-training affects not only competition-style math but also formal proofs, reasoning benchmarks, and code generation.
subtopics: Few-shot chain-of-thought evaluation on English and Chinese math benchmarks
Performance relative to open models such as Mistral 7B and Llemma 34B
Comparison to Minerva 540B and what it says about data versus parameter count
Program-aided reasoning on GSM8K and MATH using Python
Formal theorem proving via autoformalization on miniF2F with Isabelle and Sledgehammer
Results on MMLU and BBH as measures of general understanding and reasoning
Results on HumanEval and MBPP as measures of retained coding ability
Why math pre-training can improve general reasoning without sacrificing code performance
The broader lesson: domain-specific training can amplify general capabilities

outline.description: After building a strong base model, the next step is to make it follow mathematical instructions reliably. This chapter covers the design of the supervised fine-tuning dataset and the resulting DeepSeekMath-Instruct model.
subtopics: Goals of instruction tuning after continual pre-training
The 776K-example mathematical SFT dataset
English sources: GSM8K, MATH, MathInstruct, and Lila-OOD
Chinese K-12 data collection across 76 subtopics
Solution formats: chain-of-thought, program-of-thought, and tool-integrated reasoning
Training procedure: packed examples, 4K context, learning rate, and number of steps
DeepSeekMath-Instruct performance on math benchmarks without tools
DeepSeekMath-Instruct performance with tool use on quantitative reasoning tasks
Comparisons against large open-source chat models and proprietary systems
Why a 7B instruct model can compete with much larger aligned models

outline.chapter_title: From PPO to GRPO: Reinforcement Learning Without a Critic
outline.description: This chapter develops the paper's main algorithmic contribution, Group Relative Policy Optimization, by first explaining standard PPO and then showing how GRPO reduces memory cost while staying effective for mathematical reasoning.
subtopics: Why reinforcement learning is used after supervised fine-tuning
Review of PPO as an actor-critic method for language model alignment
The PPO surrogate objective and clipping mechanism
Value functions, Generalized Advantage Estimation, and their computational cost
KL penalties and the role of the reference model in stabilizing training
Why critic training is especially awkward when rewards appear mainly at the final token
The key GRPO idea: estimate the baseline from grouped outputs to the same question
The GRPO objective and group-relative advantage estimation
Direct KL regularization in the loss rather than in the reward
The unbiased KL estimator used in GRPO
Why comparative group rewards match how reward models are typically trained
Memory and efficiency advantages of GRPO over PPO

outline.chapter_title: Reward Design and Training Protocols for Mathematical RL
outline.description: Reinforcement learning depends not just on the policy optimizer but also on how rewards are assigned. This chapter explains the reward modeling choices and RL variants explored in the paper.
subtopics: Building reward models for mathematical reasoning
Outcome supervision with final-answer rewards
Group normalization of rewards within each prompt
How outcome supervision assigns the same normalized advantage to all tokens in a solution
Process supervision with step-level rewards for intermediate reasoning
Step boundary detection and per-step reward aggregation
Token-level advantage construction under process supervision
Iterative GRPO with reward-model refresh and replay of historical data
Reference-model updates and exploration loops in iterative training
Practical RL settings: number of prompts, 64 sampled outputs per question, sequence length, batch size, learning rates, and KL coefficient
Defining in-domain and out-of-domain tasks during RL evaluation

outline.chapter_title: What Reinforcement Learning Changes in DeepSeekMath
outline.description: This chapter studies the empirical effects of RL on DeepSeekMath-Instruct, including benchmark gains, transfer beyond the training distribution, and the relationship between sampling and final accuracy.
subtopics: Training DeepSeekMath-RL from DeepSeekMath-Instruct using only a subset of English CoT data
In-domain gains on GSM8K and MATH
Out-of-domain gains on benchmarks such as CMATH despite no direct RL training on them
Why the RL model surpasses open-source systems from 7B to 70B
Tool-free versus tool-assisted performance after RL
How self-consistency interacts with a stronger reasoning model
Why RL can improve benchmark accuracy even after strong supervised fine-tuning
The significance of reaching over 50% on MATH in the open-source setting

outline.chapter_title: A Unified View of SFT, RFT, DPO, PPO, and GRPO
outline.description: Beyond introducing a new algorithm, the paper proposes a general framework for understanding many post-training methods as variations of reinforcement learning. This chapter turns that framework into a teaching tool.
subtopics: The unified gradient perspective on post-training
The three ingredients: data source, reward function, and algorithm
Supervised fine-tuning as reward-guided probability shaping
Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RFT) and correctness-based filtering
Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) as preference-based direct optimization
Online RFT and the importance of sampling from the current policy
PPO and GRPO as online reinforcement learning methods
Offline versus online data sources and why online sampling eventually wins
Gradient coefficients as the mechanism for reinforcement and penalization
Why GRPO can outperform Online RFT by using richer reward magnitudes
How process supervision further sharpens the gradient signal
When seemingly different post-training methods are best seen as simplified RL

outline.description: The final chapter synthesizes the paper's empirical lessons, explains the authors' interpretation of why RL works, and highlights limitations that point toward the next generation of reasoning-focused language models.
subtopics: Evidence that code training improves mathematical reasoning with and without tool use
Two-stage versus one-stage code-and-math training
Catastrophic forgetting and why mixed training can preserve coding ability
The surprising weakness of arXiv-only training for the evaluated math tasks
Caveats to the arXiv conclusion and where it might still help
Why RL improves Maj@K more than Pass@K
The interpretation that RL strengthens output distribution alignment more than fundamental capability
The misalignment problem in supervised reasoning models
Current weaknesses in geometry, theorem proving, and few-shot learning relative to GPT-4
Potential improvements in data sources, out-of-distribution prompts, and advanced decoding strategies
Robust RL under noisy rewards and weak-to-strong alignment
Open problems in reward-model generalization, uncertainty estimation, and efficient process reward modeling
